summary:
South Jeolla Province has no separate provincial ordinance on gender identity or gender expression. A visitor to the province therefore stands under South Korea's national framework, in which being transgender is not a criminal offence in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal.

The exception sits with the armed forces. Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted. In 2017 the military criminally charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm to a trans person concerns Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available without a surgical condition. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that gender change cannot be determined by surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity.

The Supreme Court ruled en banc on 24 November 2022 that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors. A 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the principal advance in that area. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, although LGBTI organisations can register: an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government continued to appeal, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a documented live problem. On the ruling finalised on 22 July 2024, a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and made final a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink in order to do so, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that had prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom.

Schools are part of the same pattern. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed. A 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants; organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction. At Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters.

Everyday hostility is recorded in survey data. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, that 65.4% of those recommended reported harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the previous year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
No incident specific to South Jeolla appears in the sourced material; every restroom, military and recognition finding drawn here comes from courts and agencies elsewhere in South Korea and applies province-wide as national law.

The courts producing trans-positive outcomes sit at different levels of the same system, from the Yeongdong regional bench on surgical prerequisites to the Supreme Court en banc on trans parents and the Seoul appellate bench on restroom advice, while the military justice system runs the opposite direction under article 92-6.

Public-event violence is recurrent rather than isolated, with Incheon and Busan Pride as the two documented cases, and in the Incheon case organisers pursued charges against clergy while alleging police passivity.

Outing through official channels has precedent: the May 2020 contact-tracing episode and the police restroom advice both involved state actors producing exposure or restriction that courts later treated as a rights violation.
localsOnly:
Residents of South Jeolla are subject to the same national rules as visitors on criminal law and legal gender recognition, but several consequences bear mainly on those living here: no provincial or national anti-discrimination statute covers gender identity, so workplace, housing and service refusals have no general statutory remedy, and an NGO's registration fight through the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 shows the administrative route that organisations must take.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or enter a civil union, cannot jointly adopt, and gained only the limited healthcare standing recognised by the 2024 Constitutional Court ruling.

Young men living in the province face conscription under a code that criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel, while transgender people are excluded from service; the 2017 charges against 32 personnel and the six-month sentence show how article 92-6 is used.

The National Human Rights Commission of Korea received complaints on hospitalisation guidance in November 2023 and received the restroom survey data in 2021, which is the route residents can use where no statute covers the harm.

Conversion therapy is not prohibited, and the 2014 finding that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended it, with the harm and trauma figures attached, describes an unregulated practice.
outOfScopeNotes:
No South Jeolla-specific incident, ordinance, court decision or survey appears in the source inventory, so the province is scored entirely on the national framework; whether local police, schools or hospitals here behave as the national reporting describes is unresolved.

The restroom damages award is described in one source as finalised on appeal after the state's appeal was dismissed and elsewhere as a first-instance ruling with no appeal available; the outcome, 300,000 won against a 3 million won claim, is consistent across sources but the procedural posture is unresolved.

Sources do not address restroom access, school facilities or hospitalisation practice in South Jeolla's own institutions, nor whether the province operates any local support or complaint mechanism for trans residents; this is not sourced either way.

Whether article 92-6 has been enforced against personnel stationed in South Jeolla is not sourced.
